newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt sold at close on data, offshore weakness.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt sold at close on data, offshore weakness.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close

* NZ debt ends on soft note as U.S., Australian yields rise
* Labour Cost, dwelling permit data stronger than expected
* Market awaits Tuesday's Quarterly Employment Survey
New Zealand debt markets finished the week on a poor note on Friday, with yields nudging higher in the face of weak U.S. Treasuries and stronger than expected economic indicators.
Bonds finished five to six basis points weaker, while the 90-day bank bill rate closed three higher at 7.45 percent.
Sentiment was bruised by Labour Cost data at the top of market expectations. Overall salary and wage rates, including overtime, rose by 0.7 percent in the quarter and 2.0 percent in the year.
Private sector salary and wages rose 0.5 percent in the quarter (1.8 percent annually) while public sector salary and wage rate rose 1.0 percent on a quarterly basis and 2.5 percent annually.

Rates rose slightly on the back of the news, but Bancorp Treasury Services said in a statement the rise Labour Cost growth was "not significant enough to cause (Reserve Bank governor) Don Brash any heart flutters".

Bankers Trust economist Nick Bennenbroek said the numbers were slightly higher than BTNZ forecast, but were close enough to market expectations to provide no firm clues about Tuesday's Quarterly Employment Survey.
The QES is expected to attract keen interest given recent swings in employment demand, and the implications for monetary policy of wage inflation.

As well as the Labour Cost data, Statistics New Zealand also released data showing permits for new dwelling construction rose 7.9 percent in the year to January. The figures, which follow Thursday's news of a 17.1 percent rise in the value of building consents issue in the year to December, were higher than expected and marginally negative for bills and bonds.
ANZ Bank senior manager of domestic markets Jim Reardon said the 10-year bond was being rejected quite significantly each time it approached the 7.25 percent level.

"The back of the curve is coming under pressure now. It tried to flatten up yesterday and has given up some ground. I still think it will try to flatten up again but overall, the taste is that the long end of the curve is struggling every time it gets to the mid 7.20s," he said.
Reardon said the entire yield curve was running out of pace, and was not helped by global weakness.

"Outright yields are probably not going to look that good over the next couple of weeks...but we might do alright against the spread, because there is no real genuine selling of Kiwi other than as a sentiment issue," he said.
